newsitem.title: KENYA: Tanzanian flower growers to get direct cargo flights.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanian flower growers to get direct cargo flights.

text.p: Flower growers in northern Tanzania's Arusha region surrounding Mount Kilimanjaro will soon get three weekly freight flights flying their fresh produce directly to Europe, importers and freighters said this weekend.

The move is seen by the industry as a major development and is initiated by German importer Omniflora, which in the past few years has seen an increasing volume of flower imports from East Africa, especially Tanzania.

"We are planning three charter flights a week from East Africa into Europe from the end of September," Klaus Voss, Chief Executive of Omniflora said this weekend at the end of Kenya's three-day horticultural trade show, Hortec '97.

The flights will be chartered through the private Nairobi-based freight company Airlink, which is a subsidiary of Swiss freight forwarders Kuhne & Nagel and details of the routes are now in the process of being finalised, Voss said.

"The three flights will most probably start in the south, Malawi, and all stop over in Kilimanjaro airport, with one of the three flights making a third stop in Nairobi as well. From there they will fly to Ostend or Luxembourg, which have much lower landing charges than at Frankfurt," he said.

"We have decided to charter the freight flights in order to secure the transport of our flowers into the European markets. We expect to take something like 80 tonnes a week from Tanzania," Voss told Reuters late on Saturday.

He said East Africa in recent years had become the "most important flower grower" for European importers as the region had developed a reputation for producing high quality flowers, but in most countries reliable cargo routes were not available.

"East Africa has established itself in Europe because of a good quality and the variety of flowers they produce here in the region. From Kenya the transport is not a problem, but for all the neighbouring countries, they are lacking air connections.

"I personally think there is a high potential, a very great potential in the future for East African flower growers, but only if one of the big obstacles, the air freight issue, can be resolved," said Voss.
He said that while Tanzania was one of the newcomers at the flower market, the country was producing "high-quality roses".
If the Tanzanian floricultural industry was developed carefully, Voss said Tanzania could become "a major player in the horticulture market in Europe" within the near future.

"We do this new chartered flights in co-operation with Airlink, of which two thirds of the total capacity will be reserved for our own imports, while the remaining third will be offered for other flower exporters in the Arusha region.
"One of the three flights will be a DC-10, which takes some 75 to 80 tonnes, while the two other flights will be smaller aircraft with about 35 tonnes capacity each," said Voss.
